newsitem.title: USA: NYS focuses on transit budget, LIPA unresolved.
newsitem.headline: NYS focuses on transit budget, LIPA unresolved.

text.p: New York State lawmakers on Thursday focused on a huge capital program for the state transit agency as budget talks ground on, but that issue, as well as an electricity deal for Long Island, was unresolved.

Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, wanted assurances that a plan to transfer about $15 million of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority's operating funds to its capital budget would not hurt suburban county bus lines by triggering service cuts and fare increases.
"It's not a matter of as much as money, but it's matter of taking operating funds and transferring it to capital and creating an operating deficit," he told reporters.
Gov George Pataki said he thought Silver's concerns about fare increases were incorrect, adding he hoped the MTA's capital program would be approved as soon as Thursday.

The state agency wants to use some of the money to buy 1,080 new subway cars--340 more than it first expected to be able to afford--but risks having to renegotiate the deals if the capital program is not swiftly approved.

Pataki and the top two legislative leaders were grilled about whether the governor's plan for a partial take over of the Long Island Lighting Co was being held hostage by the Assembly Speaker who wanted concessions on other matters.
Neither the governor nor his Democrat opponent, Assembly Speaker, Sheldon Silver said that that was what was occurring, though both have at times been criticized for such strategies.

Pataki said "It's too important for Long Island and if the Speaker were to do that I think he would feel the wrath of Long Islanders and I think that the plan obviously works for Long Island and for New York State and I'm pleased that Senator Bruno has indicated that his party will vote yes, and I hope Speaker Silver votes yes as well."

The governor was referring to fellow Republican Joseph Bruno, Senate Majority Leader, from Troy. Pataki, Silver and Bruno each can veto the plan to have the Long Island Power Authority buy assets from LILCO and Brooklyn Union Gas, which plan to merge, with the nation's biggest-ever bond sale.

Silver said the transaction had never been discussed in relation to the budget. Bruno was not quite so definite. "We're talking about all the major things that are still out there and we're trying to move forward on--(it's) not necessarily linked, but certainly hasn't been resolved."

The state board that must approve all bond offerings, including the plan to sell about $7.3 billion of tax-exempt debt to pay for the deal, next meets on July 16. Each of Albany's top lawmakers controls one of the board's three votes, and the LIPA deal was expected to be on the agenda, though it might be pulled.

The Assembly Speaker, who blamed the state's failure to enact a budget on time on his opponents' focus on sound bites instead of substance, disagreed with Bruno's assessment that progress had been made on all the issues except prisons. The state's budget was due on April 1.

In a sign of how rancorous relations between the two houses had become, the head of the Assembly energy committee and Bruno released separate statements blaming the other side for killing a plan use low-cost power to create jobs.
